display.purpose: The wordmark only. Poetsen One ships one weight; never request 600.

headline.purpose: A site's hostname on its detail page, with the shared domain suffix dimmed.

title.purpose: A list row's hostname. The only other use of the display face.

eyebrow.purpose: Section and dialog headings, uppercase and letterspaced.

label.purpose: Card headings inside the detail page: Request path, Manual steps, Deploy, Danger.

micro-label.purpose: The label above a single routing hop. Smallest type in the system, so it takes Smoke, not Smoke Deep.

body.purpose: Explanatory sentences a person wrote. Nunito, never for paths or commands.

body-strong.purpose: The title line of a selectable option row, above the sentence explaining what the choice commits you to.

data.purpose: Machine values: hop values, detail rows, a card's path or port line.

code.purpose: Copyable commands and the generated deploy workflow.

pill.purpose: One-word state, uppercase, prefixed with a filled dot.

shadows.name: overlay
shadows.purpose: Elements genuinely fixed above the page: the flash banner. Nothing in normal document flow gets this.

shadows.name: scrim
shadows.purpose: Dialog ::backdrop. How a modal separates from the page — not a drop shadow.

motion.name: state-transition
motion.purpose: Hover and checked-state changes on cards, buttons and option rows. Gated behind motion-safe.

motion.name: copy-feedback
motion.purpose: How long a copy button shows its check icon and Copied label before reverting.

motion.name: banner-dismiss
motion.purpose: Success banner auto-dismiss. Never applied to a banner carrying an unfinished manual action.

motion.name: press
motion.purpose: Button press feedback — a 1px downward shift while the button is held. Gated behind motion-safe.

breakpoints.name: lg
breakpoints.purpose: Exists only for the add-site page's two-column frame: below it the form and what-gets-written panel stack into one column instead of sitting side by side.

breakpoints.name: rail
breakpoints.purpose: The shell's own breakpoint: at and above it the 250px rail shows beside the content; below it a top bar and a drawer replace the rail. A usable fallback for a tailnet phone, not a mobile design.

containers.name: frame
containers.purpose: The page frame: the shell's <main> and every page in it, centred in the width beside the rail, so every page shares one left edge. The site list fills it for row alignment; a site's detail page takes it as one column, its sentences held to the 25rem prose measure; the add-site page splits it into form and panel. There is no narrower reading column (a 760px one was retired 2026-10-27).

containers.name: rail
containers.purpose: The left rail at 900px and wider: Hearth, a 1px Hairline right rule, scrolling on its own; navigation only.

components.name: Service Row
components.description: The row shape of the services board, and the one place a status pill leads. A fixed-width left column holds the pill; the right column holds the unit's name on one line and its facts beneath, as prose rather than columns, with no raw reconciler result word, and the reconciler's gate string on its own line in full only for a blocked or failed run that has one. A deploy that is blocked or failed gets its own line directly under the name, '● deploy blocked · <reason>': Scorch for trouble and Smoke for a deploy that is only waiting ('deploy waiting'), colour on the 'deploy <word>' alone, set in mono, and the reason a phrase in Nunito Smoke (omitted when it repeats the word or when the gate string sits beneath the line), a blocked deploy is classified by the inventory's gate_code and never by the sentence, a failed one by its result; a blocked row with no code, or a code the app does not know, gets no line, and neither does a container row with nothing installed whose pill already reads failed or awaiting image, and the facts line never carries the result word except 'blocked' on a row whose gate_code the app cannot classify (no deploy line). Prose and not a table because half the rows have no deploy state and never will, and the longest content breaks a row grid. Each group (reconciler, services, infrastructure) is its own page, named by the page eyebrow, so there are no Micro-label group headings and no card around the rows. Age always renders as an age, never a timestamp, with no threshold. A site whose declaration is retired grows one last line, the prune line: a compact Secondary button, Prune old declaration, and a Nunito caption with its file and repository as Chalk mono facts naming the file it deletes and what it waits for. The same markup sits under a site page's detached warning, where the button is compact Primary because it is that page's next step. A unit whose inventory entry lists host actions grows the host-action strip: Start (only when not up), Restart (only when not down) and Update as compact Secondary, and Stop (Danger, only when not down) as the only coloured button, because Stop is the one action that leaves the server down and two red-family outlines side by side read as one; Stop, Restart and Update confirm inline in place of the strip, Stop in the Scorch wash and the others on Hearth Lift; the last run is a mono fact line over a 'log · N lines' disclosure, open when it failed; while a run is active the pill turns neutral naming it and every button disables. Every row has an anchor (service-<name>) for the site page to link to; a site resource's name links to its site only while that site is in the Caddyfile. A row whose pill reads unknown carries one Smoke sentence saying the state of that unit or container could not be read. A container row with nothing installed whose last run failed, or which is awaiting its first image, shows the same word its site page does, failed or awaiting image; other states can differ by design.

narrative.overview:
A console you would choose to sit in. Nearly every fact on screen is set in DM Mono — hostnames, ports, paths, commands, service names, status words, even the section labels — because nearly every fact came from a machine and will be pasted back into one. Nunito carries the sentences a person wrote, and the rail's place words. The ground is Hearth, a warm near-black with a trace of brown in it, never #000: this is a room with a lamp in it, not a void. Against that, exactly one chromatic voice — Ember — marks everything you can act on.

The density is deliberate and generous at once. There is one operator, one desktop viewport, and no competition for their attention, so nothing is folded, capped, truncated, or hidden behind a disclosure widget; a generated workflow file renders at its full height because it is a file you might read, not a blob you might copy. But the page is not a wall either — cards are tonal steps, not boxes with lines around them, and the vertical rhythm is loose enough that the four sections of a site's page read as four separate answers to four separate questions.

Components are tactile and confident: fuller padding than a dense admin panel would use, visible state changes on hover and focus, and an accent that is not shy about appearing on the things you press. Depth stays flat at rest and lifts only in response to state. Two directions are confirmed rejections: the generic dark SaaS dashboard (violet gradients, glassmorphism, KPI tiles and sparklines for metrics this app does not have) and terminal cosplay (scanlines, ASCII borders, green-on-black, faux boot logs). Mono type here is precision, not costume.
keyCharacteristics: Warm near-black ground; no pure black, no pure white — Chalk, not #fff.
One accent, Ember, reserved for what is interactive.
Mono for machine facts, sans for human sentences and the rail's place words.
Flat tonal layering at rest; shadow only as a response to state or float.
Uppercase letterspaced micro-labels as the structural device.
Nothing folded, capped, or truncated — one operator, one wide viewport.
Poetsen One as a signature, twice, small.

rules.name: The Ember Is Interactive Rule
rules.body: Ember and its family mark what you can act on — buttons, focus rings, the checked option, step numerals, a card's hover edge. It never colors a heading, a body sentence, or a value you can only read. On any given screen it covers well under 10% of the pixels, and that rarity is what makes a primary button unmissable. A control the page expects to be refused never wears it.

rules.name: The Three-Tone Status Rule
rules.body: Site state resolves to exactly three tones: Clear, Scorch, or Smoke. starting, unknown, not deployed, awaiting image and retired are Smoke, never Scorch — a container still running its first health check is not broken, a status we failed to read is not evidence that anything is down, a container that was never created (or was deliberately taken down) has not crashed, a site attached to a repository whose first image has not been deployed yet is between two steps, not failing, and a declaration deliberately retired (state: absent, not yet pruned) was taken down on purpose. Scorch is reserved for something that tried and failed, so that red keeps meaning "this needs you now": a site that has simply never been deployed must not look like one that died. Never invent a fourth tone, and never let a tone marking site state appear without the canonical status word beside it — that second clause is what makes the first safe, because the word carries which state it is while the tone carries only how bad it is. The what-gets-written panel's Clear-marked added lines are the one place Clear appears without a status word, because marking a diff addition is not a site-state verdict for this rule to govern. not deployed, awaiting image, retired and unknown share Smoke and stay unambiguous, because the word is always there to tell them apart. That is why retired exists at all: a site re-added over a retired declaration once read not deployed, the same word as a site never attached, so the shared tone hid a different state. A new state that needs telling apart gets a new word, never a new tone.

rules.name: The Pill-Needs-an-Edge Rule
rules.body: A status pill aligns to an edge the eye can follow down the page. A single-line row has a clean right edge, so the pill is right-aligned there — the site list. A multi-line row does not: its content is ragged, and a right-aligned pill floats against nothing. So a multi-line row puts the pill first, in a fixed-width left column, where the pills' left edges line up and state can be read down the page without reading a name — the services board. Same component and the same vocabulary either way; only the placement moves, and the row's shape decides it, never habit or symmetry with the other page.

rules.name: The Scorch-Is-Not-Ember Rule
rules.body: Danger uses the red family even though it neighbors rose in hue, and the two never substitute for each other. Ember means "act here." Scorch means "this destroys something." A destructive control is outlined Scorch on transparent, never filled Ember.

rules.name: The Dim-Text Rule
rules.body: Dim text is Smoke, not Smoke Deep. Smoke Deep carries readable text in exactly one role — the .lychee.land suffix on a Headline, which at 27px is WCAG large text and clears the 3:1 that applies there. At any smaller size it fails the 4.5:1 that applies instead (3.16:1 on a card), so every label, key, caption, and hop sub-line takes Smoke. When a new dim role appears, the question is not "how dim can this be" but "does it clear 4.5:1 on both Hearth and Hearth Lift." Two things are deliberately outside that test, because neither is text you read to learn something. The breadcrumb's / is decorative punctuation between two links, and is marked aria-hidden to say so. And a disabled control's label takes Smoke Deep on purpose: WCAG 1.4.3 exempts text that is part of an inactive user interface component, and dimness past the readable floor is precisely the signal that the control is not yours to press right now. That exemption is not a license to dim anything inconvenient — it applies only while the control is genuinely disabled, and it is why a disabled control must never keep a hover fill underneath it (measured at 2.09:1 the one time it did, which is unreadable rather than merely dim).

rules.name: The Mono-Carries-Facts Rule
rules.body: If a machine produced it or will consume it — hostname, port, path, command, service name, status word, framework name — it is DM Mono. If a person wrote it as a sentence, it is Nunito. The one other case is a word naming a place in the app — the rail's overview, activity, sites, host, services, reconciler and infrastructure — which is Nunito too, since it is a word and not a fact (since 2026-10-29). No sentence sets a path in Nunito: a fact inside a sentence is a mono span in Chalk, within the sentence's Nunito. A line that pairs a status word with a reason (● deploy waiting · <reason>, ● retiring · <reason>) sets the word in mono and the reason in Nunito.

rules.name: The Signature-Twice Rule
rules.body: Poetsen One appears in exactly two places: the wordmark and a list row's hostname. It is never a page heading, never above 1.5rem, never body copy, and never used for emphasis. The family also ships a single weight — do not request 600 and let the browser synthesize it.

rules.name: The Uppercase-Is-Structural Rule
rules.body: Uppercase with letterspacing marks structure, never emphasis inside prose. Tracking widens as size shrinks (0.85rem/0.08em → 0.75rem/0.1em → 0.6875rem/0.09em) so the smallest labels stay readable. Emphasis inside a sentence uses Chalk against Smoke, or <strong>, not caps.

rules.name: The Show-It Rule
rules.body: There is one operator and one wide viewport, so content is never folded, capped, truncated with an ellipsis, or put inside an inner scroll box. A generated workflow file renders at full height. One exception is horizontal overflow on a one-line command, which must not wrap: overflow-x: auto with white-space: nowrap. Long values wrap by breaking characters (break-all), never by being cut. Hostnames are the exception: a Headline holds its label whole and breaks before the domain, and a rail row shows the label alone; either breaks inside a label only when that label alone is wider than its line. Two surfaces scroll inside themselves because nothing else can reach their content: the rail, once its sites outgrow the viewport, and the find panel's result list, once it does. The activity tables — the overview's and /activity's — scroll sideways in their own box, and only below the width their five columns need; at the desktop width it never does, and the page itself never scrolls sideways. Two more are named. A finished host action's log folds at rest; it is open while the action runs and open after a failure, so the log that explains something is never behind a click. A finished runbook step folds at rest too — one line, the check, its title, done, and a chevron, the body one click away — but a step that is not done never folds, so setup in progress is never behind a click.

rules.name: The Frame-And-Column Rule
rules.body: 1080px is the page frame — the shell's <main>, and every page inside it, so every page starts at one left edge and moving between them moves nothing. No width ever lengthens a line of prose past about 70 characters: every Body sentence carries the prose measure (25rem), a cap on text rather than a second page width, so the frame can stay wide for commands, code and the request path. A page with two kinds of content that belong side by side splits the frame — on the add-site page the form column is 656px beside the panel — rather than narrowing it. The site list fills the frame because its rows need the width to align a reserved status column. Until 2026-10-27 a site's detail page centred a 760px reading column inside the frame, and its left edge jumped 160px at 1440px on every move from the list; there is no reading column now. The system holds one page width and never a second.

rules.name: The Flat-At-Rest Rule
rules.body: A surface sitting in the document is flat: tone plus a Hairline, no shadow. Shadow means one of two things — this element floats above the page, or you are touching it right now. It never means "this card is important."

rules.name: The Scrim-Owns-the-Modal Rule
rules.body: A dialog is separated by its backdrop and its border, not by a heavy drop shadow. If a modal needs more separation, darken the scrim.

rules.name: The Radius-Says-Size Rule
rules.body: 10px contains, 6px is controlled, 4px is inline, round states one word. A new component takes the step matching its role — never a value between steps, and never a large radius to look friendlier.

rules.name: The Count-Line Rule
rules.body: An overview cell is a count line, not a KPI tile: a label, a mono total with the tone chips, and one quiet fact. No hero figure, no chart or sparkline, no trend arrow, no percentage. The host has no metrics to visualize, only things that are fine, things that are not, and things nobody could read; a cell says how many of each and links to the page that names them.

rules.name: The Coupled-Inset Rule
rules.body: Every copy button in the app is one size (16px icon → 26px button) at one inset (6px), pinned center-right in a single-line block and top-right in a multi-line one. The code block's 10px vertical padding and 44px right padding are chosen against those numbers to balance the gap and keep the button off the text. Change any one of the four and recompute the others.

rules.name: The Icon-Says-Direction Rule
rules.body: In a button that pairs an icon with a text label, the icon's position states which way the action goes — not decoration. A leading icon names the action's category — plus for "this creates something", trash for "this destroys something". A trailing icon means the action leaves the app, which is why "Visit" carries external-link on the right and nothing else does. No icon means the surface you are already on has stated the action: the add-site page's submit button is a bare "Add site" because the heading above it already reads "Add a site", and a plus there would say it twice. A button never carries an icon on both sides, and a purely decorative icon is not a fourth option. An icon-only control — the copy button — and a label-only control with nothing to add, like Cancel, sit outside this rule's domain rather than counting as exceptions to it.

rules.name: The Evidence-Marks-Done Rule
rules.body: A runbook step is checked only by something the page has read, never by the operator's say-so and never by elapsed time. The commit and the first tag are done once the reconciler has found a tag in the registry; attach is done once a declaration exists, or, only when the app's copy of lychee-resources cannot be read, an inventory entry; deploy is never checked, because once something is installed the runbook is replaced. A step that cannot be verified from here stays open rather than guessing, so a check always means the host agrees.

dos: Do set every machine fact in DM Mono and every human sentence in Nunito. A path in Nunito is a bug.
Do reserve Ember for what the operator can act on, and keep it under ~10% of any screen.
Do give starting, unknown, not deployed and awaiting image the neutral Smoke tone. None of them is a failure.

Do show a status word with every tone that marks site state — the dot and the tone are never the whole message. The what-gets-written panel's Clear-marked added lines are the one exception, because a diff addition is not a site-state verdict.
Do let long hostnames, paths, and commands break or scroll (break-all, or overflow-x auto plus nowrap for one-liners).
Do put remediation beside the hop that reported the problem, not in a numbered step list.
Do check a dim tone against both grounds before using it on text: 4.5:1 on Hearth and Hearth Lift below 24px, 3:1 at or above it.
Do keep the shared focus ring: 2px Ember, 2px offset, :focus-visible.
Do gate every transition and the dialog entrance behind motion-safe.
Do state a destructive flow's steps in execution order, and say outright that a failed step stops the rest.
Do keep the copy-button fallback that selects text when navigator.clipboard is unavailable — over plain HTTP it always is.
donts: Don't fold, cap, truncate, or add an inner scrollbar to content the operator might read. One operator, one wide viewport. The two named folds are The Show-It Rule's: a finished host action's log, and a finished runbook step, at rest; its named scroll boxes are the rail, the find panel's list, and the activity tables below their width.
Don't use Poetsen One anywhere except the wordmark and a list row's hostname, and never above 1.5rem or at a weight it doesn't ship.
Don't fill a destructive button with Ember or make it the largest control on screen — Scorch outline, one size down.
Don't introduce a second accent hue, a gradient, or a chart. This app has no metrics to visualize.
Don't add a shadow to a card, a pill, or anything else sitting in normal document flow.
Don't put a status color on prose, a heading, or a background behind a sentence — status colors belong to pills, sub-lines, and error surfaces.
Don't use uppercase for emphasis inside a sentence; it marks structure only.
Don't put a status mark back on the rail's site rows or host links. The rail carries one health mark, the overview signal, and the overview page carries the rest.
Don't show a live-looking indicator for something nothing checks. Hop 1 never carries live state; every indicator on hops 2–4 is something actually checked, not invented health.
Don't auto-dismiss a banner that carries an unfinished manual action.

Don't drift toward the dark-SaaS-dashboard look (violet gradients, glassmorphism, KPI tiles — the overview's strip is count lines, per The Count-Line Rule) or toward terminal cosplay (scanlines, ASCII borders, green-on-black, faux boot logs).
